qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal for the EU Inc. appears to depart from the stakeholder-driven corporate model (Rhineland model) that exists in several Member States and to align more closely with a US-style shareholder-driven model. For instance, directors no longer appear to be required to assess decisions of the shareholders’ general meeting which go against the interests of the company before implementing them. This may be relevant, for example, where shareholders decide to distribute funds whilst the company’s financial position does not permit this. Accordingly, a discrepancy could result between the legal standards against which directors of an EU Inc. and directors of national companies are assessed. This could reduce legal certainty and the predictability of directors’ liability, particularly for individuals who are simultaneously directors of an EU Inc. and of a company governed by national law. 1.
Why is the Commission moving away from the stakeholder-driven governance model and opting for the shareholder-driven governance model?
What standard should national courts apply when assessing the lawfulness and any liability of directors of an EU Inc., and how does this relate to the various national governance models?
How will the Commission ensure legal certainty for individuals who hold directorships in both an EU Inc. and in companies governed by national law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2026) The proposal for a Regulation on the 28th Regime Corporate Legal Framework ‘EU Inc.’1 provides a flexible governance framework tailored to the operational needs of startups and scaleups across Member States. While the corporate legal framework introduced by the EU Inc. Commission proposal grants shareholders operational agility, it embeds robust financial safeguards. Specifically, Article 72(3) prevents distributions unless all directors certify in a signed statement that the company remains financially viable. When assessing actions taken by directors, national courts will have to verify whether the relevant directors have acted in accordance with the duties set out in the EU Inc. Commission proposal as well as in other applicable EU and national laws. The liability of directors is partially harmonised under Article 44 of the Commission proposal, with any further aspects remaining governed by national law. Directors’ duties depend, inter alia, on the specific legal form of a company, which often differs between private and public limited liability companies. Individuals acting as directors across several companies must comply with the applicable duties governing each respective company. This standard applies equally to individuals who accept an appointment as a director of an EU Inc. company alongside holding directorships in other corporate entities governed by national law.
1 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the 28th regime corporate legal
